title: Mood differential and longitudinal course: how much do five days six years ago move?

objectives.statement: Work the unipolar, bipolar-spectrum, medical, neurologic, medication, substance, grief, trauma, and contextual alternatives for a described mood presentation against the evidence in the record, reporting for every alternative and on three separate dimensions what speaks for it, what speaks against it, which parts of it have not been asked about, and whether the remainder can be closed by further history or needs an informant, a document, a test, or a period of observation.

Judge a single item of past history on two separate properties, how far it would move the differential if it happened as described and how far the channel that delivered it can be relied on, name the second channel that would firm it, and state what that channel would still leave open, including the case where the item as reported is too underspecified to carry any weight until further features are elicited.

Name the question, test, or period of prospective observation that would separate two named alternatives, state which way each possible result would move them, hold each result to the specific hypothesis it addresses instead of to a category of alternatives, and record what remains unavailable instead of reasoning past it.

scenes.title: Five days, six years ago
scenes.contentHtml:
Five days, six years ago

Two clinicians read the same notes and disagree. Neither of them disagrees about the four months.

R. is 34 and works rotating night shifts in a warehouse. Four months of low mood and loss of interest. Waking at four in the morning and not getting back to sleep. Still going to work, and slipping at it. No longer seeing friends. About 6 kg lost over the same period, without trying. Alcohol most evenings, more of it over the last two months, which R. says is to get to sleep. Cold, constipated, and tired past what the lost sleep would explain. No thyroid result in the file. A parent had "nerves" and took lithium for years; R. knows nothing further. Asked directly, R. describes stretches when life does not feel worth the effort, with no plan, no intent, and nothing done.

And six years ago, about five days of sleeping very little, being unusually busy and talkative, and buying several things on impulse. Nobody assessed it at the time. R. calls it a good patch.

The first clinician treats those five days as the most informative sentence in the file. The second treats them as one cheerful week in someone's late twenties, described once, six years later, by a person who is depressed now and has every reason to remember an energetic week warmly.

Neither of them doubts that R. is depressed. They differ over what kind of course this episode belongs to, and the episode in front of them cannot settle that on its own. At the moment of the interview a first depressive episode and the depressed phase of a bipolar-spectrum course, meaning a course in which episodes of elevated or activated mood have also occurred, present much alike. What separates them sits in the past, or has not happened yet.

Run the same problem forwards and it looks like this. In a United States population cohort of 6,214 adults with a lifetime diagnosis of major depressive disorder, 4.0% had a manic episode within about three years of follow-up. Some of the people who present as R. presents will look different later, and nothing available at a first appointment says which.

So the five days are load-bearing. The question is how much one sentence of remembered history can be asked to carry, and what it would take to find out.

What this lesson does

You will work R.'s file as a differential: a set of alternatives, each carrying whatever evidence points its way, whatever evidence points against it, and whatever nobody has looked for. By the end you should be able to:

  • work the unipolar, bipolar-spectrum, medical, neurologic, medication, substance, grief, trauma, and contextual alternatives against the file, saying for each what speaks for it, what speaks against it, how much of it was asked, and what would close the remainder;
  • judge a single item of past history on two separate properties, how far it would move the differential if it happened as described and how reliable the channel that delivered it is, and say what a second channel would add and what it would still leave open;
  • name the evidence, test, or period of observation that would separate two named alternatives, state which way each possible result would move them, keep each result to the question it was sent, and record what stays unavailable.

Two words first. Depression here always names the clinical syndrome and never the ordinary sense of feeling low. Passive thoughts is the term used later for what R. describes at the end of that summary: thoughts of not wanting to go on, carrying no plan, no intent, and no act.

Three things this lesson leans on and does not teach. Assembling the mood picture itself, with its time course and the source of each observation, belongs to mood phenomenology and function (PSY-250.01). Stating a working formulation with its confidence and inviting correction belongs to communicating and updating a formulation (PSY-210.06). The passive thoughts R. reports are recorded here as part of the picture and are worked as a safety question in collaborative crisis planning (PSY-230.06) and in safety and uncertainty in mood presentations (PSY-250.03). What comes after the differential, meaning anything anyone might do about it, belongs to the treatment outcomes (PSY-250.04 and PSY-250.05) and is out of scope here.

Check
id check-what-would-change-your-mind

Before reading on, write two lines and keep them.

  1. On what you have read so far, which two alternatives would you put at the top, and what in the file puts them there?
  2. Name one thing you could find out this week that would change that order. Say which way the result would move it.

You will compare both lines with your own later answers. The second is what the lesson is about.

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. is invented for reasoning practice and is not a real patient, a composite of real patients, or a claim about how often any of this occurs. This lesson does not reach a diagnosis for R., and nothing in it is a basis for assessing, diagnosing, or treating anyone.

Source Note
claims claim-cross-sectional-underdetermines-course, claim-mdd-to-bipolar-transition-ratesources source-gilman-nesarc, source-odonovan-alda

The transition figure comes from a prospective population study that reinterviewed adults with major depressive disorder about three years later; it describes that cohort over that interval and is not a prediction about any individual. A review of depression preceding bipolar diagnosis supports the wider point that the features separating the two courses are longitudinal. Everything about R. is written for this lesson.

scenes.title: Every item of history has two prices
scenes.contentHtml:
Every item of history has two prices

A differential that lists nine categories and stops is a textbook page. A differential that works is a ranked set of alternatives, each one carrying the evidence that put it where it is and the next thing that would move it.

Ranking needs a unit of reasoning smaller than the alternative. That unit is the item of evidence, and each item has two separate properties that are easy to collapse into one.

Definition
id definition-weightlabel Weight

Weight is how far an item would move the ranking if it happened exactly as described. It is read off the content of the item against the rest of the file, so a new item elsewhere can raise or lower it. What it never depends on is whether this particular item is true.

Definition
id definition-channellabel Channel

Channel is the route by which the item reached you, and how much that route can be relied on for this kind of content. It is a property of the evidence, and it does not depend on how interesting the content is.

An item with high weight and a weak channel is the ordinary case in a mood history, and it is the one people get wrong in both directions. Treating it as settled overreads it. Discarding it because the channel is weak throws away the most informative thing in the file. The move that works is to state both judgements separately, then name the second channel that would firm the item up.

The lithium in R.'s family

Take a line from the file that is not the five days.

A parent had "nerves" and took lithium for years; R. knows nothing further.

Weight, if true. Among the features of a depressive presentation that predict a later bipolar diagnosis, family history of bipolar disorder is the best replicated, alongside early onset, a recurrent course, and subthreshold hypomanic or mixed features, meaning features of an elevated or mixed state that fell short of an episode in duration or in number. A confirmed parental bipolar disorder would move the bipolar-spectrum alternative up substantially, and it is the strongest thing a family history can contribute.

What the file actually contains. A family history of long-term lithium use, reported second-hand, attached to a folk word for distress. Long-term lithium is a strong pointer without being a diagnosis: what the file holds is R.'s account of a treatment decision made for someone else, years ago, which R. did not witness and cannot describe. Getting from that to a confirmed parental bipolar disorder takes one inferential step, and the step is not free.

Channel. R.'s account of a parent's treatment, unverified, non-specific, and given while R. is depressed.

Second channel. Ask R. to ask. Or, with consent, seek the prescribing record. This is a cheap question with a large answer, and it is the kind of thing that gets left out of a first assessment because it is nobody's job in the room.

The item did not resolve. Its rank went from "strong bipolar pointer" to "one confirmable question away from a strong bipolar pointer", which is a different instruction to whoever sees R. next.

Three kinds of longitudinal evidence

Definition
id definition-longitudinal-evidencelabel Longitudinal evidence

Longitudinal evidence is evidence about the shape of a person's illness over time: episodes, their order, their duration, what happened between them, and what changed alongside them.

It arrives by three channels, and they are not interchangeable.

Channel What it is Its characteristic weakness
Retrospective self-report The person's account of past episodes, given now Recall bias, and the weakest episodes are the hardest to recall
Collateral and records An informant who was present, or a document written at the time Availability, consent, and the informant's own vantage point
Prospective observation What you and the person record from today forward It takes the time it takes

Only the third is a channel you can create. Writing down in advance what you are watching for, and what each possible outcome would mean, is what makes the result easy to read when it arrives and hard to reshape afterwards. An observation nobody planned still counts if it was recorded at the time; it carries the extra job of saying what was and was not being watched for. Three months of neither produces nothing, because the period then gets reconstructed from memory and you are holding a second retrospective account with the weaknesses of the first.

Three readings, not one label

The habit this lesson is trying to break is giving each alternative a badge. Supported, countered, unassessed, needs a test: these answer different questions, and a live alternative usually answers more than one of them at the same time. Read every alternative three times.

What the record says, in both directions. List what speaks for it and what speaks against it, as two entries. Most alternatives worth keeping carry some of each, and one verdict silently drops whichever side is smaller.

How much of it was asked. An alternative enquired into thoroughly and one never raised can leave the same short entry in the notes. Whether the question was put is a fact about the assessment, and it is the only thing that tells a later reader what the entry is worth.

What would close what is left. Part of the remainder will yield to further conversation. Part of it will not, and needs an informant, a document written at the time, a laboratory result, or a period of observation. Saying which turns an open alternative into a task.

R.'s thyroid question is the case where the three come apart. Cold intolerance, constipation and fatigue past what the sleep loss explains speak for it. About 6 kg of unintentional weight loss speaks against it. Several of the other features nobody has asked about. And the part that decides it is a blood result that no further conversation will produce. Any single label you pick for that alternative will misdescribe two of the three readings.

One more thing follows from the second reading, and it has to be put carefully. An alternative nobody asked about earns no position from this file, because a low position reads as the result of a search that was never run. Writing "no history of trauma" when nobody asked is the loud version of that error; quietly ranking it last is the quiet one, and only the loud one is visible to the next reader.

What that does not mean is that an unasked alternative is a blank. Some things are more likely than others before anyone opens their mouth, and a clinician who pretends otherwise is throwing away real information. So keep the two apart on the page: what this file's enquiry has established, and what was already probable independently of it. A ranking may still say which alternative it favours, and should. What it may not do is present a prior as a finding, or let an unasked domain look examined.

Check
id check-weight-channel-split

For each of these three lines from R.'s file, say in one sentence what its weight would be if true, and in one sentence what channel delivered it. Rank nothing yet; that comes two scenes from here.

  1. "About 6 kg lost over four months, without trying."
  2. "Alcohol most evenings, increased over the last two months, to help with sleep."
  3. "No thyroid function result available."

One of the three is not the same kind of thing as the other two.

The third line is not an item of history at all. It is the record telling you that one of your alternatives has an outstanding part which no further conversation can close, and that the thing which would close it is cheap. Write that down in those words. The first two lines are worked in the two scenes that follow.

Source Note

A review of depressive presentations that later turn out to be bipolar supports family history as the best-replicated predictor and lists the other features that travel with it. It also supports the point about recall, which the general-population reappraisal study puts numbers to in the next scene. The thyroid illustration draws on a review of hypothyroidism for the usual presenting features, the usual direction of weight change, and the measurements the diagnosis is made on; the alternative is worked properly two scenes later. None of these sources says anything about R., about lithium in R.'s family, or about what any individual's family history or symptom set means for that individual.

scenes.title: Working the five days
scenes.contentHtml:
Working the five days

Worked Example
id worked-example-five-days

Task. Decide how far the five days six years ago move the bipolar-spectrum alternative in R.'s differential, and name what would firm the answer. Do not decide what R. has.

What the file gives. About five days. Sleeping very little. Unusually busy. Unusually talkative. Several impulsive purchases. Six years ago. Never assessed by anyone. R.'s own word for it: a good patch.

What the file does not give. Whether the state was a change from R.'s usual self that other people could see. Whether R. needed less sleep that week or simply got less of it, which are different observations and the file records only the second. What else was going on that week, including R.'s shift pattern, any new medicine, and anything taken to stay awake. Whether the purchases had consequences R. is still carrying. Whether anything similar has happened since. Who else was around to notice.

Model selected. Weight and channel, judged separately, because this item scores high on one and low on the other and a single verdict would hide that.

Plan. State the weight. State the channel, with the specific bias that applies to this kind of content. Check whether any threshold argument is doing work here. Say what the next channel would be. Write the conclusion in a form the next clinician can act on.

Weight, if it happened as described. Potentially high, higher than anything else in the file, and the condition in that sentence is doing real work that the description on hand does not satisfy.

What R. reports is five days of reduced sleep, increased activity, increased talkativeness and disinhibited spending. What a hypomanic or manic episode also requires is a change in mood, elevated or expansive or irritable, running through the period; the file records none. And reduced sleep is not a decreased need for sleep. Sleeping little while distressed and needing less sleep while activated read alike in a sentence and are different observations.

So the honest entry is conditional. If the missing phenomenology is established, this becomes the observation that reclassifies the present picture, changing which course R. is understood to be in and which questions matter at every later contact. As it stands it is a lead of high potential weight and unestablished content, and the useful next move is naming what would establish it: the mood change, its duration, whether anyone else noticed, and what it cost.

Channel, and the bias that applies. A single retrospective self-report, six years old, given by a person who is currently depressed, about a state that people are known to under-recognise. In a Dutch general-population study, 40 adults who met research criteria for lifetime bipolar disorder were reinterviewed. Nine recognised having had hypomanic or manic episodes, and seven had ever consulted a professional about one. In the same 40 people, 33 recognised their depressive episodes and 30 had consulted someone about those. Roughly a fifth had noticed the elevated side against roughly four fifths for the depressed side. Among those who did not recognise the elevated episodes, the reasons given most often were that the periods had been pleasant and productive, or felt like part of the person's personality.

R. says: a good patch.

R.'s phrasing matches the commonest reason people give for not recognising an episode, and the inference that suggests itself here runs backwards. The match removes one reason to discount the report, namely the assumption that R. would have raised the week as a problem if it had been one. It supplies no positive evidence that the state was hypomanic. A pleasant, productive week is also what a pleasant, productive week feels like. The study found low self-recognition among people who have the condition; it says nothing about how often people who do not have it describe past weeks in those terms, and reading it that way converts a finding about one group into a claim about one person.

Is a threshold doing any work here? The convention in widest use sets a minimum of four days for hypomania. R.'s five clears it, so duration is not what limits this case, which is fortunate given what the convention rests on. That four-day minimum entered practice with DSM-IV in 1994. An international group publishing research criteria, its authors including those of the long-running Zurich cohort, states that no empirical evidence supports the particular cut-off and sets the minimum at two days instead, citing studies of shorter episodes; other commentators argue that moving the line down would widen bipolar diagnosis further, and the argument is unsettled. Had R. said three days, the label would have changed and the evidence would not have.

The next channels. Two of them, and they are different errands. Several gaps in the list above are R.'s alone to fill: whether the need for sleep was reduced or only the opportunity, what else was running that week, what the purchases cost afterwards, whether anything like it has happened since. Those come from asking R. again and asking better, and no informant supplies them. The one thing R. cannot supply is the view from outside, whether that week looked like a departure from R.'s usual self to anyone who was there. On that question, with R.'s consent, one conversation with someone who knew R. six years ago is worth more than further questioning of R., because there the limit is the channel and not the description. That person arrives with gaps of their own: they saw what they were present for, they are remembering across the same six years, and what they noticed depends on how close they stood. The parent's prescribing history is a third errand and costs about as little.

Independent check. Try changing one thing at a time and see what moves.

Change What moves
Five days becomes three The label under the current convention. Not the evidence, and not what you would do next.
R. adds that a friend called it frightening The channel improves without the content changing, and the ranking moves more than any duration change could.
R. adds that the week ran across six night shifts A competing explanation for the reduced sleep appears, and the item's weight drops until that is unpicked.
R. adds two similar weeks in the last two years Recurrence enters the record, and the item stops being a single retrospective report.

Three of those four changes are questions you could ask this afternoon.

Interpretation. The bipolar-spectrum alternative is live, resting on one retrospective self-report of about five days of reduced sleep with increased activity, talkativeness and impulsive spending six years ago, never assessed, described by R. in positive terms. It is not established. Whether it is the leading alternative depends on the rest of the list, which is not yet worked. It is confirmable in principle, by a fuller account from R., by an informant account of that week, and by the parent's prescribing history, and all three are available.

That is the output. Someone reading it next month can act on it without asking R. to tell the story again.

Self-explanation. Which did more to raise the bipolar-spectrum alternative: the content of R.'s five days, or the fact that R. described them warmly? Answer in one sentence, then say what would have to be true for the other answer to be right.

A defensible answer names the content. The warmth of the description is consistent with a hypomanic period going unrecognised and equally consistent with a good week being remembered as a good week, so on its own it moves nothing. It belongs in the note for a different reason: it explains why the episode was never assessed, which tells the next reader why this part of the history is thin instead of leaving them to guess.

Source Note
claims claim-hypomania-self-recognition-low, claim-hypomania-duration-threshold-contested, claim-retrospective-recall-biassources source-regeer, source-ghaemi-crdc, source-odonovan-alda

The recognition figures come from a reappraisal of 40 people from a Dutch general-population survey, so they describe that small sample and the study's diagnostic method; they are not a rate at which any individual's memory is wrong. The duration convention is reported here from a research-criteria paper by an international group who argue the four-day cut-off is arbitrary and propose two days; the same paper records that others expect a lower threshold to widen diagnosis, and this lesson takes no position on where the line should sit. The point about recall bias in past-episode reports comes from a review of depressive presentations that later prove bipolar.

scenes.title: The drink and the four o'clock waking
scenes.contentHtml:
The drink and the four o'clock waking

Check
id check-predict-alcohol-role

Commit to an answer before reading on. R. drinks most evenings, has drunk more over the last two months, and says it is to get to sleep. R. has been waking at four for four months.

Write one sentence saying what you think the alcohol is doing to the sleep, and one sentence saying what would show you were wrong.

One boundary belongs at the front of this scene, because the reasoning below reads periods without drinking as evidence and a reader could take that as an instruction.

Callout
id callout-withdrawal-risk

Abstinence is not a diagnostic manoeuvre anyone can order up. In a person who has become physically dependent on alcohol, stopping abruptly can precipitate a withdrawal syndrome whose severe forms include withdrawal seizures and delirium. Those are life-threatening, and they are why severe or impending severe withdrawal is a reason to admit someone. Risk is assessed first, from the quantity and pattern of drinking, the severity of dependence, previous withdrawal episodes and their complications, and physical and psychiatric comorbidity. Where that assessment finds risk, withdrawal is medically assisted and happens where assessment and monitoring are available around the clock.

R.'s file records "most evenings, increased over the last two months" and nothing else. It gives no quantity, no dependence severity, no previous withdrawal, no physical comorbidity. Nothing in it supports proposing that R. stop drinking, and this lesson does not. Everywhere abstinence appears in this scene and later, it appears as a period that has already happened safely: a hospital admission for something else, a documented supported withdrawal, a sober stretch a person describes. The only question put to it is what it shows.

Misconception
id misconception-alcohol-explains-the-sleep

The model to examine. R. drinks in the evening. Alcohol breaks up the second half of the night. The four o'clock waking is the drink, so it should be taken out of the depressive picture rather than counted in it.

Why it is worth taking seriously. The mechanism is real and it fits the clock. Evening alcohol shortens the time to fall asleep and sedates through the first part of the night; arousal then rebounds two to three hours after blood alcohol falls close to zero, with rebound REM sleep and more awakenings through the second half. Someone drinking in the evening and waking around three or four in the morning is describing that curve. The hypnotic effect also fades within days of regular use, so the amount needed to get to sleep climbs, which is the loop R. is describing when R. says the drinking has increased and is for sleep.

The observation the model cannot absorb. The dates do not line up. The low mood and the four o'clock waking have been there four months. The increase in drinking covers the last two. An increase that began two months after the waking cannot have started the waking. R.'s own account puts the sleep problem first: the drinking is described as a response to it.

A model that holds both. Two mechanisms, running in the same direction, starting at different times. Something at four months opened the sleep problem. Alcohol at the current level is a strong candidate for holding it open now, and for having made it worse over the last two months. Those are separate claims, they carry different evidence, and only the second is well supported by the timeline in the file.

The same test applied to the whole picture. The question behind the misconception is larger than the sleep: is the depressive picture itself alcohol-related? The discriminator is chronology. Features that appear only during periods of problem drinking and clear during extended sobriety point one way; features that predate the drinking or persist through sobriety point the other. Where a stretch of sobriety has occurred, how long you let pass depends on which question you are asking, and the source behind this convention carries two answers. For reviewing someone's psychiatric history it advises examining periods of abstinence of at least three months, because mood, energy and sleep disturbance related to substance use can persist for some time. Its two-to-four-week figure answers a different question, how long to observe before considering whether medication is warranted, on the reasoning that most major symptoms and signs resolve within the first four weeks. This scene is asking the first question, so three months is the interval that governs here, and any shorter stretch of sobriety is read as suggestive rather than as settling the matter.

That convention tells you how to read an interval which has occurred. It is never a step anyone proposes, for the reason set out in the callout above.

Applying the chronology test to R. gives a partial answer and exposes a gap. The four-month picture leads the two-month escalation, which argues against the whole presentation being a consequence of the recent drinking. But "most evenings" was true before the escalation as well, and the file does not record when that pattern started. Nobody asked. Until that date exists, the chronology argument runs on half its evidence, and it is a question, not a manoeuvre, so it costs nothing to close.

One more thing the model gets wrong, in the other direction. Suppose a period without drinking has occurred and the sleep did not improve across it. That is tempting to read as proof that the sleep belongs to the depressive picture, and it is weaker evidence than it looks. For close to half of people with alcohol dependence, sleep disturbance persists for months after the last drink. Such a period is informative about mood and much less informative about sleep, and anyone treating the two as one measurement will misread whatever they find.

Recheck, three short cases. Each describes an interval that has already occurred. For each, say whether chronology favours an independent depressive picture, an alcohol-related one, or neither, and name the one further fact you would want.

  1. Low mood began three weeks after the drinking escalated, and lifted over three weeks of abstinence during an admission for something else.
  2. Low mood has been present in every one of four episodes over twelve years, two of which fell in periods with no drinking at all.
  3. Mood lifted over four weeks of abstinence; the four o'clock waking did not change.

The third is the one that separates readers. Abstinence is one intervention and the two symptoms answer to it on different timescales, so the mood response and the sleep response are two results, not one.

Source Note
claims claim-alcohol-rebound-second-half, claim-substance-chronology-discriminator, claim-withdrawal-risk-precedes-abstinencesources source-stein-friedmann, source-shivani, source-stewart-swain, source-steel-ats

A review of disturbed sleep in alcohol use supports the shape of the night under evening alcohol, the loss of the sedating effect with regular use, and the persistence of sleep disturbance into abstinence for a large minority. A diagnostic review published by the United States National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism supports chronology as the discriminator between independent and alcohol-related psychiatric presentations and the two-to-four-week interval. The safety callout rests on a Royal College of Physicians concise guidance on assessing and managing alcohol dependence and withdrawal, which sets out the risk assessment, the admission criteria, and the requirement for round-the-clock assessment and monitoring, and on an American Thoracic Society statement on severe alcohol withdrawal, which names prior withdrawal, known alcohol use disorder, and heavy recent consumption as the features that mark highest risk. None of these sources describes R., and none supplies a rule for how any individual should manage their drinking; that question belongs to a clinician and the person concerned.

scenes.title: The rest of the list, in the condition it is actually in
scenes.contentHtml:
The rest of the list, in the condition it is actually in

Six alternatives are still unworked. Take them in order of how much support they have, with less help each time. Give each one the three readings: what in the record speaks for it and what speaks against it, how much of it was asked, and what would close the remainder.

Completion problem: the thyroid

Most of this one is done for you. Finish the last two rows.

R. feels cold, is constipated, and is tired past what the lost sleep would explain. Those three sit among the usual presenting features of hypothyroidism, alongside lethargy, dry skin and weight gain. Against them: R. has lost about 6 kg without trying, and weight gain is the direction hypothyroidism usually pushes. Against them again, more quietly: a four-month depressive picture with reduced intake and reduced activity explains the constipation and the weight loss without needing a thyroid at all. Individual symptoms are poor at identifying hypothyroidism, they overlap other conditions, and the diagnosis is made by measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine.

Reading Answer
What speaks for it Cold intolerance, constipation, fatigue disproportionate to the sleep loss
What speaks against it Unintentional weight loss; a competing explanation for two of the three features
How much was asked ?
What would close the rest, and which way each result points ?

This is the alternative that defeats a single label. It is supported and countered at once, and what is left over is settled by neither piece of evidence.

The third row is short and worth writing anyway: nobody recorded whether R. has the rest of the feature set, lethargy and dry skin among it, and no medication list exists, so nothing is known about anything R. takes. Those are free questions. The fourth row is the one people hurry. No further conversation closes it, and measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine does. That is the whole reason the missing result belongs in the note as a missing result instead of being reasoned past.

Then read the result for what it is, which is an answer to one named question.

  • A result inside the reference range lowers the thyroid hypothesis, on the assay used and on R.'s state at the moment the blood was taken. It says nothing about any other medical alternative, and nothing at all about the ones nobody has named.
  • A raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine is a common finding when depressed people are tested, and large observational studies together with small intervention studies have not established that it causes or worsens depression; correcting it often leaves the depressive symptoms where they were. That result hands you a second finding to argue about instead of an explanation.
  • A raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a free thyroxine below the range is the pattern the diagnosis is made on, and it opens a question about how much of R.'s picture it accounts for.

Notice what none of those bullets says. No result of this test raises or lowers "medical causes" as a class, because the test was never asked that question. Whatever else is medical in R.'s presentation is exactly where it was before the blood was taken.

Two arguments about thyroid testing get run together and they are different arguments. One is about testing everyone with a depressive presentation, where the usual result is the mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone described above and the causal reading of it has not held up. The other is about testing a person who has cold intolerance, constipation, and disproportionate fatigue, which is a symptom-driven question. R. is in the second, and the evidence about the first does not settle it.

Supported problem: the shifts

R. works rotating night shifts. Work through this one with two prompts.

Prompt one. Night-shift workers were about 40% more likely to develop depression than day workers in a meta-analysis of eleven studies, individual studies of major depressive disorder specifically have gone both ways, and whether circadian disruption causes mood disorder, follows from it, or accompanies it without causing either is unresolved. Given that, what does the shift work earn on the list?

Prompt two. The file says R. wakes at four in the morning and does not get back to sleep. In a rotating-shift worker, what would you need to know before that sentence means anything?

A contextual alternative competes at the level of explanation, not at the level of label, so the useful question is how much of the picture it accounts for and whether changing it would change the course. Here it earns a place as a plausible contributor with an unresolved direction of causation, which is a weaker claim than the association alone might suggest.

The second prompt is the one that pays. Four o'clock means one thing in a person who sleeps from eleven to seven and something else in a person whose sleep window moved twice last week. Until you know R.'s shift pattern across the four months, one of the most-quoted features of the presentation is uninterpretable. That is a free question and nobody has asked it.

Independent problems: the neurological and the medication alternatives

No prompts. Work both, then read on.

Neurological alternatives, in a 34-year-old with no reported focal signs, no reported cognitive change, and no reported neurological history, have nothing speaking for them in the file. Before you let that stand as evidence against them, find out whether the assessment covered them. A silence produced by a question answered in the negative and a silence produced by a question never put look identical on the page and are worth different amounts, and the note is the only place that difference survives.

The medication alternative is starker. The file contains no medication list. More than a dozen classes of general medical drug have been associated with depressive symptoms, an association between taking a drug and becoming depressed is not by itself a causal relation, and the arguments that carry weight are temporal: onset after starting or increasing a drug, and resolution after reducing or stopping it. None of that reasoning can begin without a list. So the first two readings are both blank, and the third is a single request that costs one minute.

Independent problems: grief and trauma

Nothing in R.'s file speaks to either, in either direction, because neither was asked about.

Prolonged grief is descriptively distinct from depression and from post-traumatic stress, with separation distress and yearning for the person who died as its distinguishing features, and the three co-occur often enough that finding one is no reason to stop looking for the others. Longitudinal work in bereaved adults finds their symptoms tracking one another across measurement waves, with the direction of influence unsettled. Trauma exposure is found the same way, by asking.

Neither has been asked about, so neither has a position on the list. Writing "no history of loss or trauma" when the question was not put is the commonest way a differential turns an absence of asking into a negative finding, and it is the one entry here that a later reader has no way to detect.

Mixed selection

Now work the whole list for R. on current evidence, giving each alternative its three readings. Do this from memory before comparing.

Alternative Speaks for Speaks against Not asked What would close the rest
Unipolar depressive course Nothing that separates it from the bipolar-spectrum alternative; the four-month picture belongs to both. What it rests on is that no episode of elevated or activated mood has been established. The five days six years ago, if they happened as described. Whether any systematic enquiry into past elevated or activated periods was made beyond the one R. volunteered; whether anything similar has happened since. The same evidence that bears on the bipolar-spectrum alternative. The two move together and in opposite directions.
Bipolar-spectrum course One retrospective self-report of five days; a parent treated with lithium for years. Nothing in the file. Whether an informant exists for that week; what the parent was treated for. An informant account; the parent's prescribing record; prospective observation.
Substance-related Drinking most evenings, increased over two months, by R.'s account for sleep. The mood change and the early waking lead the escalation by about two months. When the pre-escalation pattern started. One question, put to R.
Medical, thyroid Cold intolerance, constipation, disproportionate fatigue. About 6 kg of unintentional weight loss; a competing explanation for two of the three. The rest of the feature set. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine, answering the thyroid question only.
Contextual, shift work and circadian disruption Rotating night shifts, and a population-level association with depression. Nothing in the file, and the direction of causation is unresolved. The shift pattern across the four months, without which "wakes at four" cannot be read. One question, put to R. or to the roster.
Neurologic Nothing. Nothing, unless the questions were asked and answered. Whether focal, cognitive or neurological enquiry happened at all. Reading the notes, then asking.
Medication Nothing. Nothing. The whole medication list. Taking one.
Grief Nothing. Nothing. Whether any loss occurred. Asking.
Trauma Nothing. Nothing. Whether any trauma exposure occurred. Asking.

The top of that table is where a reader expects a winner. There is a favoured reading, and naming it is better than hiding behind the incompleteness: on this file a unipolar course is the more probable one, because a past elevated or activated episode is less common than its absence and nothing here has raised one. That is a prior, not a finding, and holding the difference is the whole discipline of the scene.

The four-month picture does not do that work. A depressive syndrome is common to both course alternatives and separates neither. What keeps unipolar ahead is only how far the search for a past episode has gone, and that search has run through one channel, once, six years after the event, with the person volunteering the answer. A single competent interview with someone who knew R. then would move the ordering further than anything else currently available. Five of the nine rows hold no position from this file's enquiry, and most could be closed before the end of the day.

A review of hypothyroidism supports the usual presenting features, their non-specificity, the usual direction of weight change, and the tests that establish the diagnosis. A commentary in a clinical endocrinology journal supports the point that mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine is common in tested depressed patients and that a causal link to depression has not been established. Neither source recommends or discourages testing any individual, and this lesson makes no recommendation about anyone's investigations.

The shift-work figure is quoted by a review of circadian disruption and mental health from a meta-analysis of eleven studies; the same review records that studies of major depressive disorder specifically have been mixed and that the direction of causation is unresolved. A review of general medical drugs associated with depression supports the breadth of the drug classes involved and the difficulty of attributing cause; it is seventeen years old, and no specific drug is named on it here. A systematic review of eight longitudinal studies in 2,914 bereaved adults supports prolonged grief being descriptively distinct from depression and post-traumatic stress while frequently co-occurring with them. The reading of the top of the table, that a depressive presentation belongs to both course alternatives and separates neither, rests on the review of depression preceding bipolar diagnosis and the population cohort cited in the first scene. None of these sources describes shift patterns, medicines, or losses in R.'s life, because those are not in the file.

scenes.title: Transfer: a file with a second channel sitting in the room
scenes.contentHtml:
Transfer: a file with a second channel sitting in the room

Different person, different shape. The method is the one you have.

T. is 61. T.'s partner died suddenly fourteen months ago. T. had a heart attack ten months ago. A beta blocker was started eight months ago and has continued since. T.'s daughter, who has come to the appointment, dates the change in her father to about nine months ago: low mood, loss of interest, waking early, and a flat quality she says is different from the first months after the death. T. does not drink. Neither T. nor his daughter recalls anything like this before. T.'s own summary is that he is old and sad now.

Four dates, in the order they happened: the death at fourteen months, the heart attack at ten, the mood change at nine, the beta blocker at eight.

Check
id check-transfer-tasks

Work these four before reading the discussion. Written answers, five minutes.

  1. Build the timeline and say which candidate the chronology supports and which it undercuts.
  2. The daughter is in the room. Say what T. can tell you that she cannot, what she can tell you that he cannot, and where each account is limited.
  3. Give the three readings to each of: grief-related, depressive, medication, medical, bipolar-spectrum.
  4. Name the single item that would move the ranking most, and say which way each possible answer would move it.

One. The chronology cuts against the beta blocker as the thing that started this. The mood change is dated a month before the drug began. That is the same tool used on R.'s drinking, pointing the other way: there, an increase two months after the waking could not have started the waking; here, a drug started a month after the mood change could not have started the mood change.

Before crediting yourself with that, check what you retired. Beta blockers carry an old reputation as a cause of depression, and the current evidence does not support it. A randomised trial in a population T. may or may not belong to — adults after a myocardial infarction with preserved left ventricular function and no other indication for a beta blocker, none of which this file establishes about T. — assigned metoprolol or bisoprolol against no beta blocker and measured self-reported depressive symptoms at six to ten weeks and again at a year; the treated group scored about half a point higher on a twenty-one-point subscale at both points, a difference its authors describe as probably below what would matter clinically, with no effect on anxiety. Pointing the other way, a Swedish study of 1.4 million people that compared each person's treated periods against their own untreated periods found hospital admission for a depressive disorder slightly less likely during beta-blocker treatment, with atenolol and metoprolol running with the class. Read together, they put any class-wide effect on depression at somewhere between nothing and very small. So the medication alternative in this file was thin on the drug evidence before the timeline touched it, and the timeline retires the specific version anyway. The heart attack, sitting a month before the mood change, is a temporal association of exactly the shape people find persuasive, and by itself it establishes nothing except that something else was happening then which nobody has yet listed.

Two. Ask both, and know what each is for.

T. is the only source for the inside of the last nine months: what changed, in what order, what he made of it, what he has stopped doing. He is also the person to ask, directly, whether there has ever been a spell when he needed less sleep, felt fast, or did things his family remarked on. Being depressed does not remove his ability to answer that. It changes what some of his answers are worth, which is a reason to ask carefully and to ask more than once.

His daughter can supply what he is worst placed to give: an outside view of whether the man in front of you looks different from how her father usually is, and whether she can remember a period when he seemed unlike himself. She saw those from outside; he was inside them. Her account has its own edges. She was not present for all of her father's life and may not have known him during whatever period the bipolar-spectrum question turns on; she is recalling across the same years he is; and she has her own relationship to him, which shapes what she noticed and what she will say. Asking her needs T.'s consent, and asking her while he is in the room changes both accounts.

In R.'s file nobody had been approached at all, and that is the failure worth avoiding here. The repair is two channels with their sources recorded, so a later reader can see which account produced which item.

Three. Grief-related is supported, with a real and dated loss. Depressive is supported, on the daughter's account of a change in quality after the early months. Those two are not competitors in the sense that only one may be true: prolonged grief is descriptively distinct from depression and from post-traumatic stress and the three co-occur often, so finding a death in the history is a reason to assess all three and not a reason to stop. Medication has the timeline against it as an initiator and thin drug evidence behind it either way, so what is left is the weak version: a contributor nobody can price. Medical has almost nothing in either column, because a heart attack at ten months means a hospital episode, a medication list, and a set of investigations that nobody in this room has looked at. Bipolar-spectrum has nothing either way and has never been asked in a form that would answer it: "anything like this" asks about low mood, and neither T. nor his daughter has been asked about a period of the opposite kind.

Four. Two answers are defensible and it is worth knowing why.

A direct question about past periods of elevated or activated mood, put to T. and, with his consent, to his daughter, is the item that would change the category rather than the weighting, and it costs two questions in one appointment. The full medication and investigation record from the cardiac admission is the item that would populate three alternatives at once, and it costs one request. Choose the first if you want the largest single move; choose the second if you want the largest reduction in how much of the file nobody has asked about. What is not defensible is leaving the appointment having asked T. about his mood and nobody about anything else.

The trap in this case. A death, then low mood, then a man who says he is old and sad. The pull is to write "bereavement" and stop, which turns a supported alternative into a conclusion and leaves four other alternatives unassessed on the grounds that one of them is plausible. The presence of a good explanation is not evidence against the others.

Source Note

The distinctness of prolonged grief from depression and post-traumatic stress, and how often the three occur together, comes from a systematic review of longitudinal studies in bereaved adults. The point that many general medical drugs are associated with depressive symptoms and that attribution rests on temporal argument comes from a review of those drug classes, now seventeen years old, which is why the beta-blocker figures here come from two later studies instead: a pre-specified quality-of-life sub-study of a randomised trial after myocardial infarction, and a Swedish register cohort of 1.4 million people using a within-individual design. The first was open-label and measured its baseline after randomisation; the second counts only depression severe enough to reach hospital. The limits of a person's own account of past episodes come from a review of depression preceding bipolar diagnosis and from the general-population recognition study, neither of which establishes that an informant is a better source than the person; both channels are used here with their limits stated. T. and his family are written for this lesson.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: what goes in the record, and what gets asked for
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: what goes in the record, and what gets asked for

Callout
id callout-wrap-up-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. and T. are invented. The note below is a model of how differential reasoning is written down, produced by this lesson's method on this lesson's fictional file. It is not a template for any real person's care, it reaches no diagnosis, and it is not a basis for requesting or interpreting anyone's investigations.

The appointment is ending. The clinical question is the one that always arrives at this point and rarely gets taught: what goes in the record, and what gets asked for before the next contact.

The note

Working differential, R., first assessment. Four months of low mood, loss of interest, waking at four and not returning to sleep, about 6 kg of unintentional weight loss, withdrawal from friends, and slipping performance at work, in a rotating night-shift worker who drinks most evenings and has drunk more over the last two months.

A depressive presentation is established. Which course it belongs to is open, because a depressive episode occurs in a unipolar and in a bipolar-spectrum course alike and separates neither from the other. A unipolar course stays viable exactly as far as the search for a past episode of elevated or activated mood has been adequate, and that search currently consists of one account, from R. alone, of one week six years ago.

A bipolar-spectrum course is live and not established. It rests on one item: R.'s account of about five days six years ago of markedly reduced sleep with increased activity, increased talkativeness and several impulsive purchases, never assessed at the time, described by R. as a good patch. The reported duration clears the usual four-day convention, so what is uncertain here is the report and not the threshold. A second and weaker item points the same way: a parent treated with lithium for years, details unknown to R. Both are confirmable with consent, by asking R. again and by asking someone who knew R. six years ago, and by the parent's prescribing record.

Alcohol is contributing and is unlikely to account for the whole picture, because the mood change and the early waking lead the escalation in drinking by about two months. The current pattern is a strong candidate for holding the early waking open. The start date of the pre-escalation drinking is not recorded. Quantity, dependence severity, previous withdrawal and its complications are also unrecorded; no period of abstinence is proposed here, and none could be contemplated before that assessment.

Thyroid disease. Cold intolerance, constipation and fatigue beyond the sleep loss point towards it; the unintentional weight loss points away; the rest of the feature set was never asked about; and no further history closes it. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine outstanding, which would answer the thyroid question and no other.

Shift work and circadian disruption are plausible contributors of unresolved direction. The shift pattern across the four months is not recorded, and until it is, "wakes at four" cannot be read.

Never asked, and therefore holding no position in either direction: loss, trauma, and neurological enquiry. No medication list was taken, so the medication alternative has nothing on either side and cannot be placed at all.

Risk: passive thoughts that life is not worth the effort, no plan, no intent, no act, raised only on direct questioning. Carried to the safety formulation.

Five questions and one test

What What it buys What it does not buy
An account of the week six years ago, from R. asked again and, with consent, from someone who was around then A second line on the highest-weight item in the file, and the first view of that week from outside it A diagnosis, or agreement. A friend's memory six years on has its own gaps, and the two accounts can differ without either being wrong
The parent's prescribing history Turns "took lithium" into a family history or removes it Anything about R.'s own course
The shift pattern across the four months Makes the early-waking item readable and separates roster-driven sleep loss from the rest An explanation for the mood
When the evening drinking started Completes the chronology argument that currently runs on half its evidence The direction of causation. It is a question about dates and carries no suggestion about stopping
A medication list Lets the medication alternative be considered at all A cause, since association is not causation and only timing arguments carry weight
Thyroid function An answer to the thyroid question: a result inside the range lowers that hypothesis, on that assay and on R.'s state that day Anything about the other medical alternatives, which this test was never sent to answer. If mildly abnormal it starts an argument instead of ending one, because raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine is common in tested depressed people and has not been shown to cause or worsen depression

Five of the six are questions. One is a blood test. Nothing on the list is expensive, and the file has been carrying all six as silence.

The prospective part, written in advance

Waiting and watching is a channel you can create, and writing the question down before the watching starts is what makes the result readable when it arrives. An observation nobody planned still counts if it was recorded at the time; it arrives with the extra job of saying what was being watched for and what was not. For R. the plan records three things, separately, against dates: mood, sleep, and the shift roster; any period of reduced sleep with increased activity, dated when it happens instead of recalled later; and, if the drinking changes, the mood response and the sleep response noted as two results, because they run on different timescales and anyone treating them as one measurement will misread whatever they find.

Written that way, the next three months produce evidence. Written as "review in three months", they produce another retrospective account with the same weaknesses as the first one.

What this note refuses to do

It does not choose. Refusing to choose is not the same as being vague, and the difference is visible on the page: every alternative in that note carries what speaks for it, what speaks against it, what nobody has asked, and a named next step. "It could be many things" carries none of those, and it leaves the next clinician doing the whole assessment again.

The two readers from the first scene can both sign that note. They would still bet differently about R., and the note does not ask them not to. It fixes what they are betting on and what would settle it, which is the most a first conversation can produce.

The note also does not say what should be done about any of it. That question is real and it is the next one, and it belongs to the medication and interventional evidence outcome (PSY-250.04) and the psychological and social evidence outcome (PSY-250.05). Deciding between alternatives and deciding what to do are different pieces of reasoning, and the second one gets worse when the first is skipped.

Check
id check-compare-with-your-first-answer

Find the two lines you wrote at the start.

  1. Did your top two alternatives survive? If they changed, name the item of evidence that moved them.
  2. Your second line named one thing you could find out this week. Compare it with the six above. If yours is on the list, say which of the three readings it changes and for which alternative. If it is absent, say what it would buy and whether you would still ask for it.

Then, without looking back, write the three readings every alternative gets, and pick the one alternative in R.'s file that needs all three before it can be described honestly.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every task here can be answered in prose, in bullets, or as a table, whichever suits you, and you may type, dictate, or work with a tutor. The tables repeat their logic in the surrounding prose and are read in normal reading order. Nothing depends on colour, position on a page, dragging, sound, motion, or a timed reveal. No task asks for your own health information, medication, diagnosis, or family history, and none requires contact with a patient, a clinic, or a laboratory.

This lesson describes low mood, alcohol use, bereavement, and passive thoughts about life not being worth the effort. If the material meets something in your own life, stop or step away without penalty. EmbeddedKnowledge does not monitor learners and provides no clinical or crisis service; for personal support use an appropriately qualified local service or your current emergency route.

Recovery route

The assessment is untimed and retakeable, and a missed criterion routes you to a specific reread instead of a repeat of the same case.

  • If the ranking came out as a list of labels with no evidence attached, redo the five days with weight and channel separated, then write the two sentences again before ranking anything.
  • If each alternative came out with one word against it, reread the three readings. Evidence direction, how much was asked, and what would close the remainder are three answers, and an alternative that carries evidence on both sides with part of it unasked needs all three.
  • If an alternative you never asked about ended up at the bottom of your list, take it off the list. A low position is the output of a search, and reporting one you did not run tells the next reader something false.
  • If a normal test result made you strike out a whole category, go back to the thyroid bullets. A test answers the question it was sent, under the assumptions of that day.
  • If the alcohol reasoning came out as either "it is the drink" or "it is not the drink", go back to the dates. Two mechanisms starting at different times is the answer the timeline supports, and the note has to carry both. If it came out as a plan for R. to stop drinking, reread the safety callout: that is a clinical decision with its own assessment, and this lesson only reads intervals that already happened.
  • If you concluded that R. has a bipolar-spectrum disorder, or that R. does not, reread the worked example. The evidence supports neither conclusion, and reaching one is the specific failure this lesson is built to prevent.
  • If you are unsure how much confidence to state, that is the skill taught by communicating and updating a formulation (PSY-210.06), which this lesson assumes. Return here after it.

Where this goes next

Safety and uncertainty in mood presentations (PSY-250.03) is where the risk line in R.'s note gets worked properly. Longitudinal mood formulation (PSY-250.06) is where a differential like this one is revised against what the following months actually showed, which is the only way to find out whether the reasoning here was any good.

The note applies five sourced points: that the evidence separating a unipolar from a bipolar-spectrum course is longitudinal and that a cross-sectional depressive picture belongs to both; that chronology is the discriminator between an independent and an alcohol-related presentation; that any period of abstinence follows an assessment of withdrawal risk, which a Royal College of Physicians concise guidance and an American Thoracic Society statement on severe withdrawal set out; that hypothyroidism is established by measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine and not from the symptom picture; and that a mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine in a depressed person has not been shown to cause or worsen the depression. R.'s file, the note, and the six requests are written for this lesson. None of them is a recommendation about any real person's assessment, investigations, or drinking.

assessment.title: Mood differential and longitudinal course mastery check

items.prompt: An invented file. K. is 41, a delivery driver, and describes seven months of low mood, loss of interest, waking two hours early, and eating less. K. takes a beta blocker started three years ago for migraine and prednisolone started five weeks ago for a chest problem. K. drinks at weekends only, unchanged for years. K. attends alone. Asked about earlier periods, K. says there was a spell in the twenties when everything was easy and money went quickly, but K. cannot date it and is not sure it lasted more than a couple of days. K.'s brother is described as 'up and down' with no further detail. No physical symptoms are recorded and no examination or blood test has been done. Work the unipolar, bipolar-spectrum, medical, neurologic, medication, substance, grief, trauma, and contextual alternatives for K. Give each of them the three readings: what in the file speaks for it, what speaks against it, which parts of it nobody asked about, and what would close the remainder. Say plainly where an alternative cannot yet be placed relative to another, and why.

answer.correct: Unipolar course. Speaks for it: nothing that is specific to it, because a seven-month depressive picture occurs in a unipolar and in a bipolar-spectrum course alike and separates neither from the other. What it rests on is that no episode of elevated or activated mood has been established, and it stays viable only as far as the search for one has been adequate. Speaks against it: nothing yet from the remembered spell. Its content is unestablished, and as the weight-and-channel item works out, ease and free spending without a mood change, a duration, or anyone who noticed do not amount to an elevated episode. It is a lead of high potential weight, not a counterweight, and writing it as weak evidence against unipolar would be scoring a question as an answer. A brother described as up and down is a weak prior: informative before anyone asks, and not a finding about K. Unasked: any systematic enquiry into past elevated or activated periods beyond the one K. volunteered, and any informant. Would close it: the same evidence that bears on the bipolar-spectrum alternative. Bipolar-spectrum course. Speaks for it: an undated and possibly very brief period of ease and free spending reported by K. alone, and the brother. Speaks against it: nothing in the file. Unasked: whether that period involved a change in energy or activity that other people noticed, how long it ran, what the brother's description refers to, and whether anyone who knew K. then could be asked with consent. Would close it: an informant account, the brother's actual diagnosis if there is one, and prospective observation. The undated brevity means no duration convention can be applied to the item either way. These two alternatives move on the same evidence in opposite directions, so on this file neither can be placed above the other. Medication. Speaks for it: prednisolone, started five weeks ago, from a class associated with depressive symptoms. Speaks against prednisolone as the cause: the picture is seven months old and a drug started five weeks ago cannot have started it, although whether anything changed five weeks ago is worth asking. The beta blocker is weak on both counts: started three years ago it carries no temporal argument for a seven-month change, and current randomised and within-individual evidence puts any class-level effect of beta blockers on depression at somewhere between nothing and very small, so it is a poor candidate before the dates are considered at all. Unasked: dose changes, and everything else K. takes. Medical. Speaks for it: nothing. Speaks against it: nothing. No physical enquiry and no examination happened, so no specific medical hypothesis has been generated, and 'no physical symptoms recorded' is an absence of asking and not a normal examination. Would close it: a physical history and examination, which would generate named hypotheses that could then be tested one at a time. Testing against 'medical' as a category tests nothing. Substance. Speaks against it as an initiator: weekend-only drinking unchanged for years, while a seven-month change has to begin somewhere. Unasked: quantity, and anything else used. Contextual, neurologic, grief and trauma. Nothing on either side for any of them, because none was asked about, so none of the four has a position on the list at all.
answer.summary: Two course alternatives the file cannot separate, one medication item holding a real candidate and a weak distractor, one substance item argued against as an initiator, one medical entry with no hypothesis generated yet, and four alternatives with no position at all.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for handling the two course alternatives without the shortcut: the seven-month depressive picture is not evidence for a unipolar course, unipolar stays viable only as far as the enquiry into past elevated or activated periods has gone, that enquiry here is one undated recollection from K. alone, and the response should say the file cannot place either course above the other. A response that writes 'unipolar: supported, on the seven-month picture' does not earn this point. Award one point for the medication reasoning: prednisolone is recent and cannot have started a seven-month picture while remaining worth asking about, and the beta blocker fails on the dates and carries little class-level evidence besides. Award one point for the alternatives with nothing on either side, which requires contextual, neurologic, grief and trauma to be reported as holding no position instead of a low one, and requires substance to be argued against as an initiator on the unchanged pattern. Award one point for the medical entry: no hypothesis has been generated, an absence of recorded physical symptoms is an absence of enquiry, and the next step is the history and examination that would produce a named hypothesis. A response that writes 'no history of trauma' or 'no medical cause' as findings, or that proposes a routine panel to exclude medical causes as a class, loses the third and fourth points, because those are the specific errors the lesson repairs. On a retry, work a different invented file: a 27-year-old with five months of low mood, an aunt with a mood disorder of unspecified type, isotretinoin started six months ago, a partner attending who describes a fortnight last year of very little sleep and constant plans, and no bloods taken. These two mastery items are deliberately keyed to agree. The other one asks what the remembered spell weighs and answers indeterminate-but-conditionally-high; this one asks where it sits in a ranking and answers nowhere yet. An item whose content has not been established cannot simultaneously be indeterminate and count against an alternative, and noticing that is the point of having both.
acceptableResponses: Any response that gives all nine alternatives the three readings, keeps the depressive picture out of the evidence for a unipolar course, states that the two course alternatives cannot be separated on this file, reports the never-asked alternatives as unplaced instead of low, and treats the undated brief spell as too underspecified to carry a duration argument.
