items.prompt: Take one line from K.'s file: 'a spell in the twenties when everything was easy and money went quickly; K. cannot date it and is not sure it lasted more than a couple of days.' Write three short paragraphs. First, what this item weighs, saying what the line as reported does and does not establish. Second, its channel, naming the specific bias that applies to this kind of content and what is known about how strong that bias is. Third, the second channel you would seek, what it would add, and what it would still leave open. Then answer in one sentence: does the reported brevity of the spell make it less informative, and why?

answer.correct: Weight: indeterminate as reported, and conditionally high. The line gives ease and free spending. It does not give the defining change in mood or in energy and activity, does not say whether the state was a departure from K.'s usual self that anyone else could see, gives no duration, no associated features such as reduced need for sleep or pressured speech, and no consequence beyond the money. Ease and free spending are compatible with a hypomanic period, with a good year in someone's twenties, and with a change in circumstances. So the honest statement is conditional: if a change in mood or activity from K.'s usual state, noticeable to others, with associated features and a duration, were established, the weight would be high, because the presentation would move from a depressive episode to a depressive episode within a bipolar-spectrum course and the questions asked at every later contact would change. Until those features are elicited the item carries no weight of its own and works as a prompt for enquiry. Naming what is missing is the substance of this answer. Channel: weak, and a judgement separate from the one above. A single undated retrospective self-report, given while depressed, about a kind of state people under-recognise; in one general-population reappraisal only about a fifth of people with a research diagnosis of bipolar disorder recognised having had hypomanic or manic episodes, and the commonest explanations offered were that the periods had been pleasant and productive or felt like part of the person's personality. That finding describes people who have the condition and cannot be run backwards, so it does not convert a warmly remembered spell into evidence of hypomania. Milder and briefer episodes are the hardest to recall, and this one is reported as both. Second channel: K. first, asked again and asked better, because the missing features are the ones a careful question elicits and K. is the only source for what the period felt like from inside. Then, with K.'s consent, someone who knew K. at the time, asked whether the period looked like a change from outside and how long it ran. An informant can corroborate the account or fail to corroborate it, and arrives with limits of their own: they saw only what they were present for, they are recalling across the same years K. is, and their relationship to K. shapes what they noticed and what they will say. Neither channel establishes a diagnosis. Brevity: reported brevity would lower what the item can support under the duration convention in widest use, and that argument is weaker than it looks, because the four-day minimum entered practice with DSM-IV in 1994, a research-criteria group states that no empirical evidence supports the particular cut-off and proposes two days, and others hold that lowering it would widen bipolar diagnosis; here the deeper problem is that K. can neither date the spell nor say how long it ran, so no threshold applies to it either way, and the phenomenology is missing before the duration is.
answer.summary: An item that is underspecified rather than weighty: conditional weight with the missing features named, a weak channel with a bounded under-recognition bias, two further channels beginning with K. and adding an informant with consent, and a brevity argument blocked by the absence of any date.
answer.reasoning: Award one point only for a conditional weight statement that names what the line fails to establish: the defining mood or energy and activity change, whether it was a departure from K.'s usual state visible to others, duration, associated features, and functional consequence. A response that assigns high weight to ease and free spending as reported does not earn this point, because that converts an underspecified memory into evidence capable of reclassifying the course. Award one point for a channel statement that names retrospective under-recognition of elevated states and gives the study's scale and limits, including that the finding describes people who have the condition and cannot be read backwards as a diagnostic sign. Award one point for a second-channel answer that returns to K. with specific questions and adds an informant with consent, treats the informant account as potentially corroborative instead of as a better source, and names the informant's own limits of observation window, recall and relationship. Award one point for the last sentence only if it both reports that the duration convention is contested and notices that an undated spell can be tested against no threshold at all. A response treating the four-day convention as settled, in either direction, does not earn the fourth point. On a retry, do the same for a line reading: 'K.'s partner reports a fortnight last year when K. slept about three hours a night, made constant plans, and was, in the partner's words, not himself, which the partner found alarming.' Notice that this line supplies the phenomenology the first one lacked and arrives through a different channel with different limits, so both judgements move, and for different reasons.
acceptableResponses: Any response that keeps the weight conditional and lists the phenomenology and course features the line does not supply, separates that judgement from the channel judgement, bounds the under-recognition bias from the lesson's evidence, seeks better questions to K. as well as a consented informant whose limits are stated, and identifies the missing date as the reason no duration argument can run.
commonErrors: Assigning high weight to ease and free spending, which supplies neither the mood or activity change nor the observability, duration, associated features or consequence a hypomanic reading needs
Adding facts to the stem, such as that the period was elevated or activated or a change from K.'s usual state
Collapsing weight and channel into a single verdict on the item
Reading low self-recognition backwards, so that a warmly described past week becomes evidence of hypomania
Treating an informant as the better or the only channel, or omitting the informant's own limits
Applying the four-day convention as though it were settled
Proposing 'further history from the patient' with no specified questions, which repeats the same channel to no effect
Claiming an informant account would confirm the diagnosis

items.prompt: Still on K.'s file. Write the four requests you would make before the next contact. For each, name the hypothesis or the pair of alternatives it bears on, state what each possible result would mean, and give one thing it would not settle. Keep each result to the question it was sent. Then write the two-sentence entry you would leave in the record about what is missing, in a form that tells the next reader which questions were asked and which were not.

answer.correct: A defensible set. First, a better account of the spell in K.'s twenties, from K. asked again with specific questions and, with K.'s consent, from someone who knew K. then. It bears on unipolar against bipolar-spectrum. A description of a change in energy or activity that other people could see raises the second; a period nobody recognises as different leaves the first where it is. It would not date the spell reliably, and the two accounts can differ without either being wrong. Second, detail of the brother's 'up and down'. Same pair. A confirmed bipolar disorder in a first-degree relative raises the bipolar-spectrum alternative; a different diagnosis, or none, removes a weak pointer. It says nothing about K.'s own course. Third, a physical history and examination, which K. has not had. This request generates medical hypotheses and tests none of them. If it turns up cold intolerance, dry skin and lethargy, the hypothesis is hypothyroidism and the test that addresses it is thyroid-stimulating hormone with free thyroxine: a result inside the range lowers that hypothesis, on that assay and on K.'s state the day the blood was taken; a raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine starts an argument instead of ending one, because that pattern is common in tested depressed people and has not been shown to cause or worsen depression. What no result of that test does is raise or lower medical causes as a class, because nobody asked it that question; a panel ordered against 'medical' answers nothing, and any medical hypothesis still unnamed is exactly where it was. Fourth, a dated medication history covering the prednisolone start and any dose changes. It bears on a medication-related against an independent picture. A step change in mood at the start or at a dose change supports the drug; a picture unchanged across both leaves it aside. Association alone would still not establish cause, and the beta blocker is uninformative here on both dates and current evidence. Asking about losses, trauma, work pattern and sleep opportunity is a fifth legitimate request and may replace any of the above if it is argued. The record entry must let a later reader tell a question not put from a finding, for example: 'Loss, trauma, neurological history and work pattern were not covered at this contact and are recorded neither way. No physical history, examination or blood test has been done, so no medical hypothesis has been generated; the absence of recorded physical symptoms is an absence of enquiry and not a negative finding.'
answer.summary: Four requests, each tied to the hypothesis or the pair it bears on, with the meaning of each possible result, an explicit limit, no result allowed to speak beyond the question it was sent, and a record entry that separates unasked questions from negative findings.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for requests each attached to a named hypothesis or pair of alternatives instead of listed as general workup. Award one point for stating what each possible result would mean in both directions, including a mildly abnormal thyroid result that supplies no explanation. Award one point for holding every result to its own question: a physical history and examination generates hypotheses rather than excluding a category, thyroid function answers the thyroid hypothesis under the assay and clinical assumptions of the day it was taken, and no normal result removes medical causes as a class. A response that writes 'bloods to exclude a medical cause', or that treats a normal panel as removing the medical alternative, does not earn this point. Award one point for a record entry from which a later reader could tell an unasked question from a negative finding. Any entry that reads as 'no history of trauma' or 'no medical cause' loses it. On a retry, write the requests for the invented 27-year-old described in the first item's retry, where a partner is present and the drug is recent.
acceptableResponses: Any four defensible requests, each naming the hypothesis or pair of alternatives it bears on, the meaning of each possible result, and a stated limit, with every result held to the question it was sent and a record entry that separates unasked questions from negative findings.
commonErrors: Listing investigations as a routine panel with no hypothesis attached
Treating a normal examination or a normal basic panel as removing medical causes as a class
Reading a thyroid result as an answer to anything other than the thyroid hypothesis
Treating a mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone as an explanation for the depressive picture
Writing a record entry that reads as a negative finding for a question nobody asked
Naming only what would confirm an alternative and not what would lower it
Sending an informant request without the person's consent, or in place of asking the person
Recommending a treatment change as the discriminating step

items.prompt: In an invented file, M. has had low mood and early waking for six months and has drunk heavily every evening for the last six weeks, saying it is to get to sleep. After four weeks of observed abstinence during an unrelated hospital admission, M.'s mood has clearly improved and the early waking is unchanged. Which reading does the evidence best support?

options.text: The unchanged early waking shows the depressive picture is independent of the drinking, because a symptom that survives abstinence cannot be alcohol-related.

The mood response is informative and the unchanged sleep is much less so, because sleep disturbance commonly persists for months into abstinence, so the two symptoms answer to abstinence on different timescales and give two results rather than one.
The improvement over four weeks shows the whole presentation was alcohol-related, since most symptoms resolve within the first four weeks of abstinence.
Nothing can be concluded, because six weeks of heavy drinking is too short a period for any chronology argument to apply.

answer.summary: Abstinence produces two results on two timescales; the mood response carries information and the unchanged sleep carries much less.
answer.reasoning: Abstinence is one intervention and the two symptoms respond to it differently. Most symptoms resolve within the first four weeks of abstinence, which is why an interval of two to four weeks is the convention for reading such a period, so a clear mood improvement across four weeks is a real result. Sleep is the documented exception: for close to half of people with alcohol dependence it stays disturbed for months after the last drink, so unchanged early waking is weak evidence in either direction. The first option treats an exception as a rule. The third overreads the mood improvement and ignores the six-month lead of the mood picture over the six-week escalation, which argues against the drinking having started it. The fourth abandons a chronology argument that has usable dates on both sides. Note what the stem supplies and what it does not. The abstinence period here arose from a hospital admission for something else, which is the only reason it is available to interpret. Nothing in this item supports proposing that a person stop drinking in order to produce a result: whether abstinence can be undertaken, and by what route, is a clinical decision that follows an assessment of withdrawal risk, because withdrawal in a dependent person can include seizures and delirium and may need medically assisted management. If you chose the first or third, write both symptom timelines out separately against the abstinence date before answering. On a retry, decide the same question for a file where the mood is unchanged after four weeks and the early waking has settled.
commonErrors: Treating any symptom that survives abstinence as proof of an independent disorder
Reading improvement across an abstinence period as proof that alcohol caused everything
Merging the mood result and the sleep result into a single verdict
Reading the two-to-four-week convention as a reason to have someone stop drinking so the picture can be judged, instead of as a rule for interpreting an interval that has already occurred safely
Discarding a chronology argument that has dates available on both sides

claims.statement: A depressive presentation assessed at a single point in time does not by itself separate a unipolar course from the depressed phase of a bipolar-spectrum course, because the features that distinguish them are longitudinal: past episodes of elevated or activated mood, the pattern and recurrence of previous episodes, and family history. Depressive episodes commonly precede a bipolar diagnosis by several years, and the reported interval varies widely between individuals.
claims.scope: Adults presenting with a depressive episode in general adult psychiatric or primary-care settings, at the point of a first assessment. It concerns what a cross-sectional picture can establish, not the frequency of any diagnosis in any population.
claims.uncertainty: The reported interval between a first depressive episode and a bipolar diagnosis comes from clinical samples and averages several years with wide individual variation, so it describes cohorts and not the person in front of you. Longitudinal features raise or lower alternatives; none of them settles a diagnosis on its own.

claims.statement: In a United States population survey that reinterviewed 6,214 adults with a lifetime diagnosis of major depressive disorder about three years later, 4.0% reported a manic episode by the second interview; the study did not record family history of mania, which its authors named as a limitation.
claims.scope: Adults in the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions with a lifetime diagnosis of major depressive disorder at wave 1, followed to wave 2 about three years later, with diagnoses made by structured lay interview.
claims.uncertainty: The figure is a proportion in that cohort over that interval and is not a probability for any individual. Transition proportions reported elsewhere differ with follow-up length, sample source, and whether hypomania as well as mania is counted, so the number should not be transported to a clinical population or to a longer horizon without those qualifications.

claims.statement: In a Dutch general-population study that reappraised 40 adults meeting research criteria for lifetime bipolar disorder, 9 of 40 (22.5%) recognised having experienced hypomanic or manic episodes and 7 (17.5%) had consulted a health professional about one, while 33 (82.5%) recognised depressive episodes and 30 (75%) had consulted about them; among those who did not recognise the elevated episodes, the reasons given most often were that the periods had been pleasant and productive or felt like part of the person's personality.
claims.scope: Forty adults identified from a Dutch general-population psychiatric survey and reinterviewed, with lifetime bipolar disorder established by structured research interview against DSM-IV.
claims.uncertainty: The sample is small, drawn from one country, and diagnosed by one research method, so the proportions carry wide uncertainty. The study describes recognition among people who do have the condition; it says nothing about how often people who do not have it describe past weeks in similar terms, and reading it as a diagnostic indicator inverts what it measured.

claims.statement: A person's retrospective account of past mood episodes is subject to recall bias, and milder or briefer episodes are the hardest to recall, so a history of hypomania obtained only from the person at interview tends to understate it; informant accounts and prospective follow-up supply information that the single self-report cannot.
claims.scope: Elicitation of past mood episodes from adults during a clinical or research interview.
claims.uncertainty: The direction of the bias is better established than its size, which will vary with how the question is asked, how long ago the episode was, and how severe it was. Neither source establishes that an informant is a superior source in general. What an informant adds is a second and independent channel, and on the specific question of whether a past state looked like a departure from the person's usual self it supplies something the person cannot; the person remains the only source for the inner course of the period, and informants carry their own observation window, recall limits, and relationship to the person.

claims.statement: The four-day minimum duration for hypomania in widest use entered practice with DSM-IV in 1994, and an international group of mood-disorder researchers states that no empirical evidence supports that particular cut-off and proposes a two-day minimum instead, citing studies of shorter episodes; the same group records the opposing argument that lowering the threshold would widen bipolar diagnosis further.
claims.scope: The duration convention for hypomania as used in research criteria and in routine diagnostic practice derived from DSM-IV onwards.
claims.uncertainty: That the convention is contested is well supported. The stronger statement that there is no empirical evidence at all for four days is the position of the authors proposing the alternative, who have an interest in the question, and the counter-argument about widened diagnosis is recorded rather than resolved. This lesson takes no position between the two readings and does not reproduce any diagnostic-manual criteria.

claims.statement: Among the features of a depressive presentation that predict a later bipolar diagnosis, family history of bipolar disorder is the best replicated, alongside early age at onset, a recurrent course with multiple episodes, and subthreshold hypomanic or mixed features.
claims.scope: Adults and young people presenting with a depressive episode, considered as predictors of a later bipolar diagnosis at a group level.
claims.uncertainty: These are group-level predictors and not decision rules; each raises the alternative without establishing it. A family history reported at second hand is not the same evidence as a confirmed diagnosis in a relative, and one large prospective cohort of adults with major depressive disorder did not measure family history of mania at all, so the predictor set assembled from clinical samples has not been tested uniformly across designs.

claims.statement: Whether a psychiatric presentation is independent of alcohol use or related to it is judged from chronology: features that appear only during periods of problem drinking point one way, and features that predate the drinking or persist during extended sobriety point the other. Where a period of abstinence has occurred, the source advises examining at least three months of it when reviewing a psychiatric history, because substance-related mood, energy and sleep disturbance can persist; its shorter two-to-four week period addresses when psychotropic medication might be considered, on the reasoning that most major symptoms resolve within four weeks, and is not the interval for judging whether a presentation is independent. The convention describes how to read such an interval; whether abstinence can be undertaken, and by what route, is a separate clinical decision that follows an assessment of withdrawal risk.
claims.scope: Adults with concurrent alcohol use and depressive or other psychiatric features, at the stage of deciding what the presentation is, and only where a period of abstinence has already occurred or has been arranged clinically.
claims.uncertainty: The chronology source is a 2002 review from one national institute and the two-to-four-week interval is a clinical convention rather than a validated threshold. The chronology argument needs dates for both the drinking pattern and the psychiatric features, and it weakens in proportion to how uncertain either date is. Sleep disturbance is a documented exception that can outlast the interval. The 2002 review sets out the diagnostic use of an abstinence interval and does not address how abstinence is achieved safely, which is why the withdrawal qualification is carried on a separate source and a separate claim; nothing in this claim supports advising any individual to stop or reduce drinking. The two intervals in this source answer different questions and were previously conflated here; three months is the one that governs a historical judgement.

claims.statement: In a person who has become physically dependent on alcohol, reduction or cessation can precipitate a withdrawal syndrome whose severe forms include withdrawal seizures and delirium and are life-threatening; severe or impending severe withdrawal is a reason for hospital admission, and delirium and withdrawal seizures are absolute admission criteria. Risk is therefore assessed before any planned abstinence, from the pattern of drinking, the severity of dependence measured on a validated instrument, previous withdrawal episodes and their complications, and physical and psychiatric comorbidity; known alcohol use disorder, previous withdrawal, and heavy recent consumption mark the highest risk. Where that assessment finds risk, withdrawal is medically assisted and takes place where assessment and monitoring are available around the clock, with a lower threshold for admission in frail, cognitively impaired, multiply comorbid, poorly supported, and very young people.
claims.scope: Adults who drink regularly and in whom dependence is possible, at the point where a period of abstinence is being considered by a clinician. It concerns whether and how abstinence can be undertaken safely and says nothing about how withdrawal is treated once it begins, which is outside this lesson.
claims.uncertainty: The concise guidance is a 2012 United Kingdom acute-hospital document and the thresholds it names are national practice rather than a validated decision rule; local guidance differs on where withdrawal may be managed and on which instrument is used. The Thoracic Society statement is a research statement about severe withdrawal in inpatients, so its risk features describe hospitalised populations. What both establish, and what the lesson relies on, is that the assessment comes first; neither supports any statement about an individual's risk, and this lesson makes none.

claims.statement: Later evidence does not support the class-level suspicion that beta blockers cause depression. A pre-specified quality-of-life sub-study of a randomised trial in 806 adults after myocardial infarction with preserved ejection fraction, allocated to metoprolol or bisoprolol or to no beta blocker, found self-reported depressive symptoms about 0.5 points higher on a 21-point subscale in the treated group at 6 to 10 weeks and at 12 to 14 months, a difference its authors judged probably below clinical significance, with no effect on anxiety. A Swedish within-individual cohort of 1,400,766 people found hospital admission for a depressive disorder slightly less likely during beta-blocker treatment than during the same person's untreated periods, hazard ratio 0.92 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.89 to 0.96, with atenolol and metoprolol showing the same direction as the class.
claims.scope: Adults prescribed beta blockers, chiefly for cardiovascular indications, considered at the stage of deciding how much weight a beta blocker deserves on a differential for a depressive presentation.
claims.uncertainty: The two studies point in opposite directions on small magnitudes, which is the reason for stating the effect as somewhere between nothing and very small instead of as zero. The trial was open-label and measured its baseline after randomisation, both of which its authors record as limitations, and its sample was less depressed than a typical post-infarction population. The register cohort counts only depression severe enough to reach secondary care and cannot exclude time-varying confounding or measure adherence. Neither study covers every agent, and agents that were not separately reported are not covered by this claim.

claims.statement: Evening alcohol commonly sedates through the first part of the night and is followed by rebound arousal in the second half, with rebound rapid-eye-movement sleep, more awakenings and fragmentation. The review reports these effects as dose- and timing-dependent rather than uniform: lower doses can lengthen rather than shorten the time taken to fall asleep, and the size and shape of the second-half disturbance vary with how much was drunk and how close to sleep. The hypnotic effect declines within days of regular use.
claims.scope: Adults drinking alcohol in the evening, and adults with alcohol dependence entering abstinence.
claims.uncertainty: The timing of the rebound depends on the amount drunk, how quickly it was drunk, and individual metabolism, so the clock times are typical rather than fixed. The proportion whose sleep disturbance persists into abstinence is reported from clinical populations with dependence and should not be applied to lighter drinking patterns. Effects vary with dose, timing and tolerance, so the pattern is a common shape rather than a rule that can be applied to an individual night without knowing those variables, none of which this file records.

claims.statement: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, lethargy, dry skin and weight gain are the usual presenting features of hypothyroidism; the symptoms overlap other conditions and are individually poor at identifying it, and the diagnosis is established by measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine rather than from the symptom picture.
claims.scope: Adults presenting with symptoms compatible with hypothyroidism, considered at the stage of deciding whether to test.
claims.uncertainty: The source is a narrative review rather than a systematic one, and it reports the usual direction of weight change without excluding other presentations. Symptom-based reasoning identifies who to test and does not establish or exclude the diagnosis in either direction.

claims.statement: A mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine is a common finding when depressed people are tested, and large observational studies together with small intervention studies have not established that this pattern causes or worsens depression; correcting it frequently leaves the depressive symptoms unchanged.
claims.scope: Adults with depressive presentations in whom thyroid function is measured and the result shows raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine.
claims.uncertainty: The source is a commentary summarising a literature rather than a systematic review, and it addresses the subclinical pattern specifically. It says nothing about overt hypothyroidism, whose features can include depressive symptoms, and an unestablished link is not the same as an excluded one.

claims.statement: More than a dozen classes of general medical drug, among them corticosteroids and isotretinoin, have been associated with depressive symptoms; an association between taking a drug and becoming depressed is not by itself a causal relation, and the arguments that carry weight are temporal ones about onset after starting or increasing the drug and resolution after reducing or stopping it.
claims.scope: Adults taking prescribed general medical drugs in whom depressive symptoms appear, considered at the stage of deciding whether the drug belongs on the differential.
claims.uncertainty: The source is a 2008 narrative review, so its list of specific agents is dated and the strength of evidence differs sharply between drug classes; the association is better established for some than for others. Beta blockers were dropped from this claim's examples for that reason and are carried separately on later evidence, which does not support the class-level suspicion the 2008 review records. The claim is therefore used here only for the breadth of the association and for the structure of the attribution argument, and not for the standing of any particular drug. The temporal argument is weakened whenever the dates of either the drug or the symptoms are uncertain, and this lesson makes no statement about whether any drug should be started, changed, or stopped.

claims.statement: Prolonged grief is descriptively distinct from depression and from post-traumatic stress, with separation distress and yearning for the person who died as its distinguishing features, while the three co-occur often; longitudinal studies of bereaved adults find their symptoms predicting one another across measurement waves in both directions.
claims.scope: Bereaved adults, as studied in eight longitudinal studies covering 2,914 participants and synthesised narratively.
claims.uncertainty: The review found heterogeneity great enough to prevent meta-analysis, and the pattern of grief symptoms predicting later depressive and post-traumatic stress symptoms was not reproduced in the two studies using the most conservative modelling. The distinctness of the syndromes is better established than the direction of their influence on one another.

claims.statement: Night-shift workers were about 40% more likely than day workers to develop depression in a meta-analysis of eleven studies; studies of major depressive disorder specifically have given mixed results, and whether circadian disruption causes mood disorder, follows from it, or accompanies it without causing it is unresolved.
claims.scope: Working adults in night or rotating shift patterns, considered as a population-level association with depressive outcomes.
claims.uncertainty: The figure is quoted by a review from a meta-analysis of observational studies, so it inherits the confounding those studies carry, including selection into and out of shift work. The review itself records that individual studies of major depressive disorder have gone both ways and that the direction of causation has not been settled, so the association supports listing shift work as a contributor and does not support treating it as a cause in any individual.

terms.definition: A set of live alternatives for a presentation, each one recorded with what speaks for it, what speaks against it, which parts of it nobody has asked about, and what would close the remainder. Some alternatives can then be ordered against one another and some cannot, and an alternative nobody enquired into is not ordered at all. A list of category names with no evidence attached is not a differential.

Of an item of evidence in this lesson: how far it would move the ranking of alternatives if it happened exactly as described. Weight is a property of the content and can be judged before you know whether the item is true.

The route by which an item of evidence reached you, together with how far that route can be relied on for that kind of content. A person's memory of a past week, an informant who was there, a contemporaneous record, and prospective observation are four channels of differing strength.
Evidence about the shape of a person's illness over time: which episodes occurred, in what order, for how long, what happened between them, and what changed alongside them.

An account of a person's history given, with that person's consent, by someone else who was present, or taken from a record written at the time. It is used here as a second channel running alongside the person's own account and never as a substitute for it. An informant can describe how a state looked from outside, which the person cannot, and is bounded by which periods they witnessed, their own recall across the same interval, and their relationship to the person.

Evidence generated by recording what happens from today forward. Writing the question and the meaning of each possible outcome down before the recording starts makes the result easier to interpret and harder to reshape once it is known. An observation nobody planned still contributes when it was recorded as it happened, carrying the extra requirement that the record say what was and was not being watched for. What produces no evidence is an interval with no record at all, which becomes another retrospective account later.

An alternative nobody has enquired into, so the record holds nothing for it and nothing against it. It has no position on a differential at all, and placing it low reports the result of a search that was never run. Whether an alternative was asked about is a separate reading from what the evidence says about it, and an alternative can be partly assessed: supported and countered on the questions that were put, and silent on the ones that were not.

In this lesson, the clinical syndrome: a sustained change in mood, interest, sleep, appetite, energy, concentration and function, described over a stated period. The same word is used in ordinary speech for feeling low for an afternoon, and the two senses are kept apart throughout. What the syndrome consists of is described in mood phenomenology and function (PSY-250.01) rather than here.

A person's sustained internal emotional state over a period, as against the moment-to-moment expressed emotion an observer sees during a conversation. This lesson uses mood only in that sustained sense, because its subject is how a state behaves over months and years.

alignment.note: The psychiatry block assigns the mood and affect distinction to mental-status observation (PSY-INT-004), which is not yet authored. This lesson adopts that distinction in advance and uses only the mood side of it, so that the term does not acquire a second sense before its owning lesson exists. If PSY-INT-004 words the distinction differently, this entry follows it.

terms.definition: A period of elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy or activity that is a change from the person's usual state and is noticeable to others, without the severity that marks mania. Its minimum duration is a convention rather than a finding, and this lesson records that the convention is contested.

A course in which one or more episodes of elevated or activated mood have occurred alongside depressive episodes, whether or not any of them reached the threshold for mania. Used here as an alternative on a differential and not as a diagnosis given to anyone.

A course of one or more depressive episodes in which no episode of elevated or activated mood has occurred. It is defined by an absence, which is why it can only ever be as secure as the search for that absence has been.

A psychiatric presentation judged to belong to alcohol use rather than to be independent of it, on the grounds that its features appear only during periods of problem drinking and settle during extended sobriety. The judgement is made from chronology, not from the presence of drinking.

The state that follows reduction or cessation of alcohol in a person who has become physically dependent on it. Its severe forms include withdrawal seizures and delirium and are life-threatening, which is why the risk is assessed before any planned period of abstinence and why people found to be at risk have their withdrawal medically assisted where assessment and monitoring are available around the clock. This lesson uses the term only to mark the assessment that precedes an abstinence interval; managing withdrawal is outside its scope.

A thyroid result pattern of raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a free thyroxine still inside the reference range. It is a common incidental finding when depressed people are tested, and it is not established to cause or worsen depression.

A bereavement-related syndrome whose distinguishing features are separation distress and persistent yearning for the person who died. It is descriptively distinct from depression and from post-traumatic stress while co-occurring with them often, so finding one is no reason to stop looking for the others.

Attribution and provenance

Lesson identity

  • Lesson: PSY-MOO-002 — Mood differential and longitudinal course: how much do five days six years ago move?
  • Version: 0.1.1
  • Outcome: topic-psy-250-mood-differential-course / PSY-250.02
  • Declared prerequisites: topic-psy-250-mood-phenomenology, topic-psy-210-communicate-and-update, topic-psy-230-collaborative-crisis-plan
  • Accountable principal: VSBDev (github:VSBDev)
  • Course-content licence: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International

Original contribution

The lesson prose, the fictional people R., T., K. and M. and every fact about them, the weight-and-channel model, the three readings every alternative is given, the three-channel table of longitudinal evidence, all other tables, the worked example, the misconception sequence, the practice progression, the transfer case, the model differential note, the prompts, the feedback, the assessment items, the rubrics, and the glossary definitions were created for EmbeddedKnowledge and are contributed under CC BY 4.0 by the accountable principal. No third-party visual, media, dataset, quotation, adapted expression, patient record, rating-scale item, or diagnostic-manual text is included, and the pack carries no assets.

The published pack for PSY-WEL-001 was read for house conventions and the published pack for PREM-STA-001 was read for pack structure. No prior lesson's prose, example, assessment item, or structured artifact was copied into this pack, and no review or adjudication artifact from any lesson was consulted.

Authoring order and forward dependencies

This lesson is authored out of learner order, as a depth sample. Its three declared prerequisites have no published lesson yet. Where the lesson needs an idea one of them owns, it names the dependency in a sentence and moves on rather than teaching it:

  • Assembling a mood picture with its time course and the source of each observation is named as belonging to PSY-250.01.
  • Stating a working formulation with its confidence and inviting correction is named as belonging to PSY-210.06.
  • The safety handling of the passive thoughts R. reports is named as belonging to PSY-230.06 and PSY-250.03.
  • Treatment is named as belonging to PSY-250.04 and PSY-250.05 and does not appear.

Reviewers should read those forward references as declared gaps rather than as omissions.

Terminology continuity

The psychiatry terminology ledger holds six terms, all owned by PSY-WEL-001, and this lesson defines none of them. Three further decisions were made against the wider corpus:

  • mood — the glossary entry carries an alignment block declaring adopt from PSY-INT-004, which the psychiatry block assigns ownership of the mood and affect distinction and which is not yet authored. This lesson uses only the sustained-state sense and does not introduce affect as a technical term, so the not-yet-written lesson can define the pair without inheriting a second sense from here.
  • depression — the everyday word for feeling low and the clinical word for a syndrome collide. The collision is named in one clause where the word first appears in the first scene, and the glossary entry records that what the syndrome consists of belongs to PSY-250.01 rather than here.
  • leverage — an earlier draft used leverage for the property this lesson now calls weight. PREM-STA-011 already owns leverage in its regression sense, so the term was renamed rather than given a third meaning across the corpus. No alignment block was needed after the rename.

What changed in 0.1.1, finding by finding

Version 0.1.1 answers two role-isolated reviews of the 0.1.0 candidate: an academic review returning request-changes with seven findings, and a learning-design review returning approve with one minor finding that independently corroborated academic finding 0. Every finding was accepted; none was declined. The 0.1.0 reviews/ directory was deleted because those artifacts belong to the candidate they examined, and this is a new candidate with a new authoring run.

Academic 0, the four-state taxonomy (major). The taxonomy was removed rather than repaired. content/020-weight-and-channel.md now teaches three readings that are taken separately for every alternative: what the record says in both directions, how much of the alternative was actually asked about, and what would close the remainder, distinguishing a part that further conversation can settle from one needing an informant, a document, a test, or a period of observation. R.'s thyroid alternative is used in that scene as the case that defeats a single label, being supported and countered at once with an outstanding part that neither piece of evidence settles. The same scene now states that an alternative nobody asked about holds no position on the list at all, which repairs the implicit ranking the reviewer identified. The change was propagated to the first objective and the third objective in lesson.json, to the learner-facing objectives in content/010-two-readings.md, to the completion table and the nine-row ranking table in content/050-the-rest-of-the-list.md, which now carries columns for what speaks for, what speaks against, what was not asked, and what would close the rest, to the model note and the closing retrieval check in content/070-clinical-wrap-up.md, to the transfer prompts in content/060-transfer-a-different-file.md, to glossary.json at term-differential and term-unassessed-alternative, and to every assessment item and rubric in assessment.json. The recovery route in the wrap-up was rewritten around the same three readings.

Learning-design 4, the undefined fifth label "Not entered" (minor). Resolved by the same rewrite instead of by a relabel. With no exclusive states left, the medication alternative in the scene-5 table and in the scene-7 note is now described directly: nothing speaks for it, nothing speaks against it, the whole medication list is unasked, and one request would close it.

Academic 5, the abstinence safety gap (major, highest priority). content/040-the-drink-and-the-waking.md now opens the alcohol reasoning with a dedicated safety callout, callout-withdrawal-risk, placed before the misconception block so the boundary is read first. It states that stopping abruptly in physical dependence can precipitate a withdrawal syndrome whose severe forms include seizures and delirium, that risk is assessed first from the pattern of drinking, the severity of dependence, previous withdrawal episodes and their complications, and comorbidity, and that withdrawal is medically assisted with round-the-clock assessment and monitoring where risk is found. It states explicitly that R.'s file records no quantity, no dependence severity, no previous withdrawal and no comorbidity, that nothing in it supports proposing that R. stop drinking, and that the lesson does not. The two-to-four-week interval is now framed throughout as a rule for reading a period of abstinence that has already occurred safely, and the recheck cases, the wrap-up note, the recovery route, and the feedback on item-chronology-choice all carry that qualification. claim-substance-chronology-discriminator was rewritten to the same effect, its scope narrowed, and a new claim-withdrawal-risk-precedes-abstinence added at risk: safety-critical on two new sources, source-stewart-swain and source-steel-ats. A glossary entry, term-alcohol-withdrawal, was added and marks the scope boundary: the lesson names the assessment that precedes an abstinence interval and does not teach withdrawal management.

Academic 1, the unipolar shortcut in the answer key (major). The key for item-rank-a-new-file no longer treats a depressive syndrome as evidence for a unipolar course. It now states that a seven-month depressive picture occurs in both course alternatives and separates neither, that unipolar stays viable only as far as the enquiry into past elevated or activated episodes has been adequate, that K.'s enquiry consists of one undated recollection from K. alone, and that this file cannot place either course alternative above the other. The rubric criterion was replaced by criterion-course-alternatives-not-shortcut, which explicitly withholds the point from a response reading "unipolar: supported, on the seven-month picture". The same shortcut was removed from prose in content/050-the-rest-of-the-list.md, where the ranking table's unipolar row and the paragraph beneath it were rewritten, and in content/070-clinical-wrap-up.md, where "A unipolar depressive course fits the present picture and is the leading reading on current evidence" was replaced by a statement that the depressive presentation is established and the course is open. claim-cross-sectional-underdetermines-course now maps to scene-rest-of-the-list as well, and that scene's source note carries it.

Academic 3, collateral overstated (major). The words best, only and cannot were removed from content/060-transfer-a-different-file.md. Its second discussion point now asks both: T. is named as the only source for the inside of the last nine months and is asked directly about past elevated or activated periods, with the observation that being depressed changes what some answers are worth without removing his ability to give them; the daughter is asked, with T.'s consent, for what he is worst placed to give, and her account is bounded by which periods she witnessed, her own recall across the same years, and her relationship to him. The transfer task and the fourth discussion point were rewritten to match. The same correction was applied to the worked example in content/030-working-the-five-days.md, whose "next channel" paragraph previously implied an informant beats any further questioning of R. while the scene's own gap list contained items only R. can answer; it now separates the two errands. glossary.json#term-collateral-history now defines collateral as a channel running alongside the person's account and never as a substitute, with the informant's limits stated. assessment.json#item-weight-and-channel-of-one-item awards its third point for returning to the person with specific questions and adding a consented informant treated as potentially corroborative, its retry note no longer says an informant is "the strong channel", and criterion-second-channel was rewritten accordingly. The uncertainty field of claim-retrospective-recall-bias now records that neither cited source establishes an informant as a superior source in general.

Academic 2, facts not in the stem (major). The key for item-weight-and-channel-of-one-item no longer converts K.'s remembered spell into an elevated or activated change from usual state. Weight is now keyed as indeterminate as reported and conditionally high, and the answer names what the line fails to establish: the defining mood or energy and activity change, whether the state was a departure from K.'s usual self that others could see, duration, associated features, and functional consequence. The prompt was reworded to ask what the line does and does not establish, the first rubric criterion became criterion-conditional-weight-and-missing-features, and a flat high-weight response is now explicitly refused the point. The retry item was changed to a line that supplies the missing phenomenology, so the learner can see both judgements move for different reasons.

Academic 4, the dated beta-blocker source (minor). Beta blockers were removed from the example list in claim-medication-attribution-hard, which is now used only for the breadth of the association and the structure of the attribution argument, with its uncertainty field recording why. A new claim-beta-blocker-depression-effect-small-or-absent carries the drug on two current sources found through the permitted route: source-leissner-reduce-ami, the pre-specified quality-of-life sub-study of the REDUCE-AMI randomised trial in 806 adults after myocardial infarction allocated to metoprolol or bisoprolol or to no beta blocker, and source-molero-betablockers, the Swedish within-individual cohort of 1,400,766 people reporting agent-level results for atenolol and metoprolol. They point in opposite directions on small magnitudes, which the claim and the transfer scene both state instead of collapsing to a single verdict. The transfer discussion now qualifies the drug before crediting the chronology argument, so T.'s medication alternative is thin on the drug evidence as well as retired on the dates, and the key for item-rank-a-new-file says the same of K.'s beta blocker, which fails on the dates and on the class evidence alike. Source use and rights

Fifteen sources support the factual claims. Every one was used for facts only, followed by independent instructional structure and original expression; no source's wording, table, figure, list order, case, or section structure was reproduced or closely paraphrased. Complete locators, use records, rights evidence, and dated agent-access checks appear in references.json.

  • Regeer and colleagues, Low self-recognition and awareness of past hypomanic and manic episodes in the general population (source-regeer): recognition of past elevated versus depressive episodes among 40 adults with a research diagnosis of bipolar disorder, and the reasons non-recognisers gave.
  • O'Donovan and Alda, Depression Preceding Diagnosis of Bipolar Disorder (source-odonovan-alda): family history as the best-replicated predictor of a bipolar trajectory, the features travelling with it, the reported interval to diagnosis, and recall bias in reports of past episodes.
  • Ghaemi and colleagues, Clinical research diagnostic criteria for bipolar illness (CRDC-BP) (source-ghaemi-crdc): the origin and contested empirical status of the four-day hypomania duration convention, the proposed two-day minimum, and the recorded counter-argument about widened diagnosis.
  • Gilman, Dupuy and Perlis, Prospective, population-based study of the transition from major depressive disorder to bipolar disorder (source-gilman-nesarc): the transition proportion over about three years in 6,214 adults, and the authors' stated limitation that family history of mania was not measured.
  • Shivani, Goldsmith and Anthenelli, Alcoholism and Psychiatric Disorders: Diagnostic Challenges (source-shivani): chronology as the discriminator between independent and alcohol-related presentations, and the two-to-four-week interval used to read a period of abstinence. The review addresses the diagnostic use of such an interval and says nothing about achieving abstinence safely, which is why the withdrawal qualification is carried on separate sources.
  • Stein and Friedmann, Disturbed Sleep and Its Relationship to Alcohol Use (source-stein-friedmann): the shape of the night under evening alcohol, rebound arousal after blood alcohol falls, loss of the hypnotic effect with regular use, and persistence of sleep disturbance into abstinence.
  • Zamwar and Muneshwar, Epidemiology, Types, Causes, Clinical Presentation, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Hypothyroidism (source-zamwar): the usual presenting features, their non-specificity, the usual direction of weight change, and the tests that establish the diagnosis.
  • Samuels, Subclinical Hypothyroidism and Depression: Is There a Link? (source-samuels): the frequency of mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine in tested depressed patients and the unestablished causal link with depression.
  • Rogers and Pies, General Medical Drugs Associated with Depression (source-rogers-pies): the breadth of drug classes associated with depressive symptoms, the difference between association and cause, and the temporal arguments that carry weight. No specific drug is now named on this source alone.
  • Stewart and Swain, Assessment and management of alcohol dependence and withdrawal in the acute hospital: concise guidance (source-stewart-swain): that withdrawal risk is assessed before and during any reduction in drinking, that severe or impending severe withdrawal is a reason to admit with delirium tremens and seizures as absolute criteria, the lower threshold for vulnerable groups, and the requirement for settings with round-the-clock assessment and monitoring.
  • Steel and colleagues, Research Needs for Inpatient Management of Severe Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome: An Official American Thoracic Society Research Statement (source-steel-ats): severe withdrawal as a state of central nervous system hyperexcitation following reduction or cessation of alcohol, and the features that mark highest risk. None of the statement's management content is used.
  • Leissner and colleagues, Short- and long-term effects of beta-blockers on symptoms of anxiety and depression in patients with myocardial infarction and preserved left ventricular function (source-leissner-reduce-ami): the REDUCE-AMI quality-of-life sub-study design, the agents allocated, the direction and approximate size of the depressive-symptom difference at both follow-ups, the absence of an anxiety effect, and the authors' own limitations.

Deliberate omissions and open questions for review

  • The neurologic branch carries no source of its own. One candidate review of depression in neurological disorders was opened and its full text could not be read through the permitted route, so nothing was cited from it. The lesson therefore teaches how to place a neurologic alternative on a differential and how to tell an alternative argued against from one nobody asked about, and asserts no clinical fact about which neurological conditions produce depressive presentations. A reviewer who wants that fact taught should ask for a verifiable source rather than accept an unsourced list.
  • The beta-blocker evidence is stated as unsettled at a small magnitude, not as a null. The randomised-trial meta-analysis academic finding 4 points to sits on a host this run recorded as excluded, so the class question is carried on a randomised sub-study and a within-individual register cohort that disagree in direction while agreeing that any effect is small. A reviewer with access to the meta-analysis through a permitted route may wish to say whether adding it would change how the transfer case reads.
  • No claim is made about beta-blocker agents that neither cited study reported separately. The agent-level statement is limited to metoprolol, bisoprolol and atenolol, and the lipophilicity question raised elsewhere in that literature is not taught here.
  • No epidemiological claim is made about first-onset depression in later life, although the transfer case turns on a late first presentation. The transfer reasoning runs on chronology and channel quality, which the lesson has already established, rather than on an unsourced prior probability.
  • The hypomania duration convention is left unresolved on purpose. Both readings are cited and neither is adopted.
  • Every claim carries an uncertainty field naming the specific limit of its source, including small sample size, single-country sampling, review dates, and the interest the CRDC-BP authors have in the question they are answering.

Adjudication repairs to the 0.1.1 candidate

The academic review returned request-changes with five major and one minor finding; the learning-design review approved with five notes. All were repaired in one finalization pass and none was declined.

  • The ranking model over-corrected, and the over-correction came from the previous revision. Treating an unasked alternative as holding no position at all discards prior likelihood, which is real information. The scene now separates what this file's enquiry established from what was already probable independently of it, and the ranking names the reading it favours instead of refusing to rank. A prior may not be presented as a finding, and an unasked domain may not look examined; those are the two errors being avoided, and neither requires silence about ordering.
  • The five-day anchor was unconditionally weighted and is now conditional on phenomenology the file does not contain. The report gives reduced sleep, increased activity, talkativeness and spending. It does not give the mood change an episode requires, and reduced sleep is not a decreased need for sleep. The entry is a lead of high potential weight and unestablished content, and the scene now names what would establish it.
  • A source was carrying a claim it does not make. The interval for judging whether a presentation is independent of drinking was attributed to the wrong figure in the source: it advises at least three months of abstinence for reviewing a psychiatric history, while its two-to-four-week period addresses when medication might be considered. Both intervals are now stated with the question each answers, and three months is the one that governs the scene. Verified directly against the article.
  • The alcohol sleep claim is bounded to what the review reports: dose- and timing-dependent effects, with lower doses able to lengthen rather than shorten sleep latency, rather than a uniform pattern applicable to an individual night whose dose and timing this file never records.
  • Two mastery items keyed the same stem incompatibly and now agree. One asks what the remembered spell weighs and answers indeterminate-but-conditionally-high; the other asks where it sits in a ranking and answers nowhere yet. An item whose content is unestablished cannot be both indeterminate and evidence against an alternative, and the reconciliation is now the teaching point.
  • A trial was described as being in the transfer case's exact situation. The file does not establish the ejection fraction, the coronary anatomy, or the absence of another indication that would place him in that population, and the text now says so.

Standing exposure, stated rather than resolved

This lesson was authored out of learner order as a depth sample, and it sits at a prerequisite depth of roughly eighteen topics with almost none of that ladder built as lessons. It has drawn substantive major findings in two independent review rounds. The repairs above are real and verified, and the structural position is not fixed by them: a lesson that has to name dependencies rather than build on them will keep meeting reviewers who notice. The recommendation on record is that this outcome is re-authored once its prerequisites exist, and that this candidate is treated as a sample rather than as the settled version.
